title: An animated icon leaves the app as an animated SVG
goal: An icon that swings is only useful if it still swings when somebody drops it into a web page. Exporting one writes a small SVG file that carries the motion as text, stays sharp at every size, and the hand-off sheet says in plain words what survives the trip and what does not.
notes:
Slice 5 of 5 from the answered study. Sits on top of the static SVG export already in the queue, and on the motion model from a-layer-can-be-told-to-change-one-of-its-propert.

MOCK: docs/design/mocks/pages/icon-export-anim-wt.html. The destination-first sheet is the one shared claim in the study NOT yet proved on the video side, so treat it as an icon-side design here rather than a settled cross-feature pattern.

SHAPE OF THE OUTPUT: a cycle in the app maps to percentages on the way out, because that is what CSS keyframes and SMIL keyTimes take. Milliseconds on screen, percentages in the file.

Known limit worth saying in the sheet rather than hiding: an icon referenced from an img tag runs its own CSS and SMIL, while a code host that inlines the SVG may strip it.
acceptance: Exporting a document whose layers move writes an SVG that animates when opened in a browser, with no picture embedded in it
The motion, the repeat, the curve and the colours survive, and the file is small enough to read
The sheet asks where the file is going before it asks for a format, and says which parts of the motion the chosen destination cannot carry
A document with nothing moving still exports exactly the static SVG it does today

log.note: deps set: the motion model lands first, then this
core writer lands: 26 tests green. Motion goes out as SMIL, one lap shared by every motion, stated as fractions of it. Adversarial review of the mock is in the notes below.

adversarial review of the mock, before building: (1) the mock's format list offers Lottie and Video and the app can write neither, so picking a README would have handed somebody a dead button; destinations now map only onto what the app can actually write, and a README gets a picture. (2) the mock's 'same thing as a GIF, 74 KB' would have been an invented number, cut, real byte size shown instead. (3) the mock ticks 'currentColor kept' and the exporter writes real colours, cut. (4) the mock's open question (change the format for you or only warn) is answered by doing both: the destination moves the format and says why, the picker stays put. Shortest version that keeps the value: the destination row only appears when something in the drawing actually moves, so Export is untouched for everyone else.

left rough (not filed, no person would hit it): a turn on a layer that is ALSO flipped or skewed is dropped rather than turning about the wrong thing, and so is a colour or width change on an inside/outside line, which the file draws in two halves. Both are named on the Export sheet before you save.
